items.title: Why We Rebuilt Microsoft Office From Scratch for AI Agents - Yijia Liang, Compound AI
items.content_snippet: Yijia Liang spent years as a finance analyst living in Excel and PowerPoint before founding Compound to build autonomous AI analysts for institutional investors. Personal agents took off because they run reliably in the background, act on their own and connect to your context, but finance needs more: multiplayer agents with their own inboxes that join deal-team email threads, a headless Office engine rebuilt from scratch with agents (1.5 trillion tokens and over 8 million lines of code) that run

items.title: Most of Your Docs Readers Are Now AI Agents - Hahnbee Lee, Mintlify & Lincoln Murr, Coinbase
items.content_snippet: In this fireside chat, Mintlify co-founder and CTO Hahnbee Lee and Coinbase head of AI product Lincoln Murr discuss what changes when agents, not people, are the main users of your product. Lee shares that agent traffic on Mintlify docs sites grew from about 10% to about 80% this year, why page size and accuracy now matter more than design, and where AI writing fits. items.title: If Your AI Scores 100%, Your Eval Is Wrong - Ramakrishnan Lokanathan, eslams.com
items.content_snippet: Ramakrishnan Lokanathan, an AI safety researcher and former startup founder, lays out how to build evals for high-stakes AI applications. Define the most ambitious version of success, test every step of the workflow and not just the final answer, combine automated checks with human review and adversarial tests, keep testing what used to work so upgrades don't break it, and turn real user failures into new tests. items.title: Your AI Agent Wants Your Data. Here's How to Lock It Down - Jeff Smith, Oracle
items.content_snippet: Jeff Smith has built database tools at Oracle for 25 years, and he's here to make agents and databases get along safely. items.title: Everyone Has the Same AI Models. Here's What Sets Agents Apart - Richmond Alake, Oracle
items.content_snippet: Richmond Alake was talking about agent memory before most people had heard of it, and now he argues the next layer after the control plane is an intelligence plane: what an agent knows, what it remembers, what it's allowed to see, and how it gets better. Using the WWII codebreakers who worked out that "AF" meant Midway, he shows why having the same information as everyone else isn't the same as intelligence.
